summary: Communication researchers compare four agent architectures (a custom monolithic Claude agent, a five-stage LangChain chain, a three-role CrewAI crew, and AutoGPT), all on Claude Sonnet 4 with the same web-search tools, across 50 journalism research tasks run once each (200 trials). They report architecture effects on duration and step counts, a non-significant accuracy difference, and different transparency profiles, interpreted through gatekeeping theory.

claims.claim: Multi-agent collaboration achieved the highest accuracy (84.7%)
claims.evidence: §4.1 Table 2: CrewAI 84.7% vs 76.9/75.5/70.6%, but one-way ANOVA F(3,196)=2.43, p=.066, eta^2=.04, i.e. not significant; the abstract omits this. Accuracy is keyword matching/semantic similarity against author-written ground truth.

claims.claim: Architecture explains 82% of variance in computational strategy
claims.evidence: Step counts are largely fixed by framework design (LangChain 15.0 steps with zero variance, §3.1), so eta^2=.82 is close to tautological rather than a behavioural finding.

claims.claim: Monolithic agent rejects 71.7% of consulted sources, mirroring human gatekeeping; framework systems hide filtering
claims.evidence: §4.2: only the custom Claude agent logged consultation; other frameworks' search wrappers did not log, so no comparison is possible. This is an instrumentation artifact of the authors' implementation.
§4.3: composite transparency differences are small (F(3,196)=2.89, p=.036, eta^2=.04); dimension weights (0.30/0.25/0.20/0.25) chosen by authors; scoring procedure for dimensions not validated.

patterns.note: Three-role CrewAI crew had highest mean accuracy at ~2x duration, but the difference was not statistically significant.
Monolithic single-model agent comparable on accuracy and best on logging visibility.
Argues framework abstraction layers obscure decision traces; based on missing logging in the authors' own integration.

methodology.sample: 50 tasks (10 per difficulty level) x 4 architectures x 1 repetition = 200 trials
methodology.baselines: Architectures compared to each other; framework versions LangChain v0.1.0, CrewAI v0.1.0, AutoGPT v0.5.0
methodology.variance: SDs reported across tasks; no repeated runs; ANOVA treats same tasks across agents as independent groups rather than repeated measures

standards.artifacts: No code, prompts, tasks or ground truth released (none found in text)

biases.detail: Accuracy by keyword/similarity matching; step-count variance is determined by framework design.
Abstract headlines 84.7% accuracy for multi-agent without stating the effect was non-significant.
One run per task-architecture; 10 tasks per difficulty level.
No tasks, ground truth, or implementations released.

coi.affiliations: College of Media and Communication, Texas Tech University (all authors)
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Open-source frameworks and Claude; no author affiliation with them

verdict_reason: off-topic: journalism research agents, not software engineering; and the headline multi-agent accuracy advantage is not statistically significant (p=.066), with a single model, single runs and no artifacts.
applicability: Does not transfer to the Java ingestion harness. The only usable point is a caution: wrapping tools inside agent frameworks can hide the decision trace (which sources/inputs were consulted and dropped), so if the team adopts a framework or mixed agent hosts it should require tool-call-level logging independent of the framework. The paper provides no evidence that role-based multi-agent setups improve outcome quality.
